Low Season: A Boat for Two Plans
He came home to sell the boat. She's the one leaving in March.
A man comes home to sell his late father's boat and finds the mechanic who kept it running — and her own route on the last page of the notebook they once wrote together.

Finn Callahan is back in Gull Harbor, Maine, for the first time in nine years, to sell the Marguerite. Lena Marsh has kept that boat alive the whole time, and on March 1 she leaves on a delivery job down the coast — her own route, written on the last page of the notebook they filled together at twenty-two. Finn wants to stay; he just doesn't know how to do it without asking her to. You decide what Lena shares, what she won't trade, and whether two plans can run side by side.
The harbor friend who runs the fuel dock — you've watched both of them leave before.
If nobody says it plainly, the boat gets sold as a memory, and Lena gets asked to become one.

For Sale, Barely Used
Get the real reason he's selling
The town dock, the Marguerite's slip
Tuesday, 3:40 PM
November in Gull Harbor: half the slips empty, the co-op closed by four. A FOR SALE sign is zip-tied to the rail of the Marguerite.
I've got a listing half-written on my phone. 'Lightly used. Well kept.' I just need her to move the toolbox out of the shot.
I don't move the toolbox. I've rebuilt that engine twice. Those scuffs on the gunwale are his dad's boots.
I'm trying to sell it.
And I'm trying to repair the life you left here.
That lands somewhere under the sweater. It was his. I put it on this morning without thinking, and now I can't take it off in front of her.
Nine years gone, and he comes back with a phone and a sign. He hasn't said why. Not once.
What does Lena do?
Ask him the real reason. Wait for it.
Why are you selling, Finn? Not the listing version.
Because I can't afford to keep her. And I can't stand keeping her when I don't know how to sail her.
I move the toolbox. Not out of the shot — onto the dock, so he has somewhere to sit.
Lena asked why he's selling; Finn admitted he can't afford the boat and can't bear to keep it unsailed.
Talk price first. The why can wait.
Fine. Business first. She's worth more than you think and less than your broker thinks. I'll give you a real number.
And the rest?
The rest you tell me when you're ready. Not in a listing.
Lena gave Finn an honest price estimate and left the reason for later.
Refuse to stage it. The scuffs stay.
Take the pictures yourself. The scuffs stay. Anyone who wants her clean can buy a clean one.
She walks up the dock. The toolbox is in every photo. Eventually Finn stops trying to crop it out.
Lena refused to help stage the boat; the listing photos show the wear.
The Last Page
Read the page she added
The Marguerite's cabin
Tuesday, 6:20 PM
Rain on the cabin roof. A space heater, a thermos, and on the chart table a spiral notebook with a warped cover. Finn knows his own handwriting from across the cabin.
It's the route we wrote at twenty-two. Portland to the islands, a page a harbor, my terrible drawings of fish.
You kept it.
I added to it.
I thought—
I know. That's why you should read the last page.
I turn to it. Her handwriting, not mine. A different route. Leaving March 1. There's no second name on it.
He'll either ask me to stay or ask me why. I can work with one of those.
Finn is reading your page. What does Lena do?
Tell him what it is. All of it.
It's a delivery job. Other people's boats, down the coast, a repair at every stop. Six months. It's mine.
That's — it's good. It's really good.
Engine comes apart tomorrow at seven. If you want to know what you're selling, bring coffee.
Lena explained her own route to Finn and invited him to the engine teardown at seven the next morning.
Let him read alone. Leave the hatch open.
I climb out into the rain and leave the hatch open, so it's clear I'm coming back.
I read it three times. At the bottom, in pencil, very small: 'Marguerite — engine seized again. Fix before March? 7 AM Wed.'
Seven tomorrow. She didn't write my name. She didn't write 'don't come,' either.
Lena let Finn read the last page alone; he found her note about fixing the engine Wednesday at 7 AM.
Take the notebook back. Not tonight.
I take the notebook out of his hands and tuck it inside my jacket.
You don't get the last page for free. Show up at seven tomorrow, help me pull that engine, and maybe I'll read it to you.
Lena took the notebook back and told Finn to earn the last page by helping pull the engine at seven.
Coming Back
Count the real costs — separately
The boatyard, the Marguerite on jack stands
Wednesday, 7:05 AM
Frost on the tarp. The Marguerite sits on jack stands with her engine half out. A coffee goes cold on the transom.
I've been up since four doing math. Rent here. Jobs here. Months until March.
I could stay. Get her running, do charters in summer. You wouldn't have to take some stranger's boat to Florida.
I set down the wrench. Slowly, so it doesn't sound like I'm throwing it.
Coming back doesn't make you the destination.
I don't know how to stay without asking you to.
It's the most honest thing he's said in nine years. It's also a request that I shrink.
What does Lena do with that?
Do the math together. Keep both plans.
I tear two pages out of the back of the notebook. One for him, one for me.
Your costs on yours. Mine on mine. Nobody's plan gets to be the other one's budget.
I write 'rent,' 'job,' 'boat?' — with a question mark. It's the first honest list I've made in years.
Lena and Finn each wrote out their own costs on separate pages, keeping both plans.
Let him sell. Talk once he's settled.
Sell her if you need to. Get a job, an apartment, a life that isn't waiting on my calendar. Then call.
That's not a no.
It's not a yes either. It's an order of operations.
Lena told Finn to sell the boat and settle his own life before they talk about anything else.
Shut it down. Your route isn't negotiable.
Lena. Remember the night we wrote that route? You said you'd never go without—

She slides back under the engine. He drinks his cold coffee. Whatever dinner might have happened this week doesn't.
Lena refused to reopen her route; when Finn leaned on old memories she shut it down, and the week's dinner didn't happen.

The Buyer
Each decides what the boat and the work are for
The town dock
Saturday, 11:00 AM
The buyer drives up from Connecticut in a car that has never met salt. He likes the Marguerite. He especially likes the price.
I have three options on a napkin. Sell. Keep her and run summer charters out of Lena's shop. Sell and take the harbor job.
Which choice gets me you?
The one where you stop asking that.
I laugh, because it's true, and because the buyer is standing right there.
His boat, his call. I'm here because I know where the leaks are, and I won't lie about them.
The buyer's waiting. What does Lena do?
Tell the buyer every leak. Honestly.
Port side weeps at the stuffing box. Engine's been rebuilt twice. She's honest. So's the price.
Disarmed, the buyer makes a fair offer. Finn says he'll decide by Monday — his decision, and he says so out loud.
Lena told the buyer every flaw; he made a fair offer, and Finn said he'd decide by Monday on his own.

If you keep her, my shop maintains her for charters. My rates, in writing. It's a business offer, not a reason to stay.
A business offer. Understood. I'll price it out.
Lena offered to maintain the boat for charters as a strictly business arrangement; Finn will price it out.

I step off the dock and go back to my shop. His boat. His call.
I sell her at a fair price. When I bring Lena the signed papers, she just says, "Good," and means it.
Lena left the decision to Finn; he sold the boat at a fair price.

The harbor office steps
